“He is young and strong. There are kisses enough for all of us.” I lay still, watching beneath my eyelashes in an agony of pleasurable expectation. The fair girl came forward and leaned over me until I felt her breath moving against me. In one way it was sweet, sweet as honey, sending the same tingling through my nerves as her voice. But beneath that sweetness was something bitter and repellent, like the smell of blood.

I dared not lift my eyelids, though I could see perfectly beneath my lashes. She knelt beside me and bent over me, openly savouring the sight. Her deliberate sensuality thrilled and disgusted me at once. Arching her neck, she actually licked her lips like an animal. In the moonlight I could see moisture shining on those scarlet lips and on the red tongue moving over sharp white teeth. Her head sank lower and lower. Her lips passed below my mouth and chin, seeming about to close on my throat. Then she stopped. I heard the wet movement of her tongue licking teeth and lips, and felt her hot breath on my neck. The skin of my throat began tingling, as skin does when a hand about to tickle it draws closer and closer. Her lips touched that exquisitely sensitive skin, soft and trembling. I felt the hard pressure of two pointed teeth, barely touching, pausing there. I closed my eyes in a languid ecstasy and waited—waited, my heart pounding.

At that instant another sensation flashed through me like lightning. I knew the Count was there, surrounded, it seemed, by a storm of rage. My eyes opened without my willing them to. His powerful hand seized the fair woman’s slender neck and pulled her back with a giant’s strength. Fury transformed her blue eyes; her white teeth snapped in anger and her pale cheeks burned red with passion. But the Count! I had never imagined such wrath, even in the demons of hell. His eyes actually blazed. A lurid red light shone from them, as though hellfire burned behind them. His face was deathly white, its lines rigid as drawn wires. The heavy eyebrows joining above his nose looked like a shifting bar of white-hot metal. With a violent sweep of his arm he flung the woman away. Then he gestured at the others as if beating them back—the same commanding movement I had seen him use with the wolves. His voice was low, almost a whisper, yet it seemed to slice through the air and ring around the room:—

“How dare any of you touch him? How dare you even look at him when I forbade it? Back, all of you, I say! This man is mine! Take care how you interfere with him, or you will answer to me.” The fair girl turned to reply with a laugh of coarse flirtation:—

“You have never loved anyone yourself. You never love!” The other women joined her. Their hard, empty, joyless laughter rang through the room until I almost fainted at the sound. It seemed the delight of devils. After studying my face closely, the Count turned and answered in a soft whisper:—

“Yes, I too am capable of love. You yourselves know that from the past, do you not? Well, I promise you this: when I have finished with him, you may kiss him as much as you wish. Now go! Go! I must wake him; we have work to do.”

“Are we to get nothing tonight?” one of them asked with a quiet laugh. She pointed to the bag he had thrown on the floor, which was moving as though something alive lay inside. He answered with a nod. One woman sprang forward and opened it. Unless my ears deceived me, I heard a gasp and a faint cry, like a child half suffocated. The women gathered around it while I watched, appalled. Then, before my eyes, they disappeared, taking the dreadful bag with them. There was no doorway nearby, and they could not have passed me unseen. They seemed simply to melt into the moonbeams and drift through the window. For an instant I saw their dim, shadowy shapes outside before they faded altogether.
Then the terror was too much for me, and I collapsed unconscious.

chapters.title: Chapter IV
paragraphs: JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL—continued

I woke in my own bed. Unless everything had been a dream, the Count must have carried me back. I tried to settle the question, but could find no certain answer. There were small clues, certainly: my clothes had been folded and put aside differently from my usual way. My watch had not been wound, although winding it is invariably my last act before bed. There were many little things of that kind. But none proved anything. They might only show that I had not been in my usual state of mind, and for one reason or another I had certainly been deeply disturbed. I must look for proof. One thing comforts me: if the Count carried me here and undressed me, he must have done it hurriedly, because nothing in my pockets has been disturbed. Surely he would not have tolerated a mystery like this diary. He would have seized it or destroyed it. Looking around the room, I find that although it has frightened me so much, it now feels almost a sanctuary. Nothing could be worse than those dreadful women who were—who are—waiting to drink my blood.

18 May.—I went down to examine that room again in daylight. I must know what is true. At the top of the stairs I found the door shut. It had been driven against the frame so violently that some of the wood had splintered. I could see that the lock’s bolt was not engaged, but something was securing the door from inside. I fear it was no dream, and must act on that assumption.

19 May.—I am certainly caught in the trap. Last night, in his smoothest voice, the Count asked me to write three letters. The first was to say my work here was almost finished and that I would leave for home in a few days. The second would announce that I was leaving the morning after its date; the third, that I had left the castle and reached Bistritz. I longed to rebel. But while I remain so entirely in his power, openly quarrelling with him would be madness. Refusing would only make him suspicious and angry. He knows I have learned too much, and that I must die or become a danger to him. My only hope is to gain time and preserve whatever opportunities remain. Something may yet happen that lets me escape. In his eyes I saw traces of the gathering fury that appeared when he threw the fair woman away from him. He explained that the post was infrequent and unreliable, and that writing now would reassure my friends. The later letters would wait in Bistritz until their dates arrived. If circumstances allowed me to extend my stay, he said, he would stop them being sent. He gave these assurances so emphatically that objecting would have aroused further suspicion. I therefore pretended to agree and asked what dates I should use. After a moment’s calculation he answered:—
“Date the first 12 June, the second 19 June, and the third 29 June.”
Now I know how long I have left to live. God help me!

28 May.—There is a possibility of escape, or at least of getting a message home. A group of Szgany have arrived at the castle and set up camp in the courtyard. These Szgany are gipsies; my book contains notes about them. They belong particularly to this region, though they are related to ordinary gipsies throughout the world. Thousands live in Hungary and Transylvania, almost entirely beyond the law. Usually they attach themselves to a powerful nobleman or boyar and adopt his name. They are fearless, have no religion beyond superstition, and speak only their own varieties of the Romany language.

I intend to write home and try to persuade them to post my letters. I have already spoken to them from my window, hoping to make their acquaintance. They removed their hats, bowed and made many gestures, but I understood these no better than their spoken language....

The letters are written. I used shorthand for Mina’s; in Mr. Hawkins’s I simply asked him to contact her. I have told Mina about my position, but left out the horrors I can only suspect. Opening my whole heart would shock and frighten her to death. If the letters fail to get through, at least the Count will not yet discover my secret or how much I know....

I have handed over the letters. I threw them through the bars of my window with a gold coin, using whatever gestures I could to ask that they be posted. The man who picked them up pressed them to his heart, bowed and tucked them into his cap. That was all I could do. I slipped back to the study and began reading. Since the Count has not appeared, I have written this....
The Count has arrived. He sat beside me and, opening two letters, spoke in his smoothest tone:—

“The Szgany gave me these. I do not know where they came from, but naturally I shall attend to them. Look!”—he must already have examined it—“one is from you to my friend Peter Hawkins. The other”—opening its envelope, he caught sight of the unfamiliar symbols, and his face darkened while his eyes burned with malice—“the other is a disgraceful thing, an insult to friendship and hospitality! There is no signature. Well! It can be no concern of ours.” Quite calmly, he held both letter and envelope in the lamp’s flame until they burned away. Then he continued:—

“Your letter to Hawkins I shall, of course, forward. Your correspondence is sacred to me. Forgive me, my friend, for breaking the seal without realising. Would you enclose it again?” He offered me the letter and, with a polite bow, a fresh envelope. All I could do was write the address again and silently return it. As he left, I heard a key turn gently in the lock. A minute later I tried the door. It was locked.
An hour or two later, the Count returned so quietly that his arrival woke me: I had fallen asleep on the sofa. His manner was very courteous and cheerful. Noticing that I had been sleeping, he said:—

“So you are tired, my friend? Go to bed; that is where you will rest best. I may not be able to enjoy a conversation tonight, for I have much work to do. But please, get some sleep.” I went to my bedroom and lay down. Strangely enough, I slept without a dream. Despair brings a calm of its own.

31 May.—On waking this morning, I decided to take some paper and envelopes from my bag and keep them in my pocket. Then I could write if an opportunity arose. But once again I met a surprise, another shock!

Not a scrap of paper remained. All my notes were gone, including my memoranda about trains and travel, my letter of credit—everything, in fact, that might help me if I got outside the castle. I sat thinking for a while. Then an idea came to me, and I searched my travelling case and the wardrobe where I had put my clothes.
My travelling suit had disappeared, along with my overcoat and rug. I could find no trace of them anywhere. This seemed to point to some fresh plan of wickedness....

17 June.—This morning I sat on the edge of my bed, racking my brains. Outside I heard whips cracking and horses’ hooves pounding and scraping up the rocky path beyond the courtyard. Full of hope, I rushed to the window. Two large leiter-wagons entered the yard, each pulled by eight strong horses. At the head of every pair stood a Slovak in a broad hat, a great studded belt, dirty sheepskin and high boots, carrying his long staff. I ran to the door, intending to go down and reach them through the main hall, which I thought might have been opened for their arrival. Another shock awaited me: my door had been fastened from outside.

I ran back to the window and shouted to them. They stared up blankly and pointed. Just then the Szgany “hetman” came out. Seeing them point towards my window, he said something that made them laugh. After that, nothing I tried—no pitiful cry, no desperate appeal—could make them so much as look at me. They deliberately turned their backs. The wagons carried large square boxes with thick rope handles. These were plainly empty, judging by how easily the Slovaks moved them and the hollow sound they made when roughly shifted. After unloading them into a great pile in one corner of the yard, the Slovaks received money from the Szgany. They spat on it for luck, then each sauntered back to his horse’s head. Soon I heard their cracking whips fade into the distance.

24 June, before morning.—Last night the Count left me early and locked himself in his own room. As soon as I dared, I hurried up the winding staircase to the south-facing window. I meant to watch for him, because something is happening. The Szgany are staying somewhere inside the castle and carrying out some kind of work. I know this from the distant, muffled sounds I occasionally hear, like picks and spades at work. Whatever they are doing must be intended to complete some merciless act of villainy.

I had watched for less than half an hour when something emerged from the Count’s window. Drawing back, I looked carefully and saw his whole body come out. It shocked me afresh to recognise my own travelling suit on him. Across his shoulder hung the dreadful bag I had seen the women carry off. There was no mistaking what he had gone to seek—and wearing my clothes! So this is his new plan: other people will believe they have seen me. He can create witnesses who think they saw me in the towns and villages posting my own letters, while making the local people blame me for whatever crimes he commits.
I am furious to think this can happen while I remain shut up here, a prisoner in every sense, yet denied the protection of the law that even a criminal can claim as his right and consolation.

I decided to wait for the Count’s return and sat stubbornly by the window for a long time. Then I noticed curious little specks drifting in the moonbeams. They looked like the smallest particles of dust, whirling together into hazy clusters. Watching them soothed me, and a kind of calm crept over me. I settled back more comfortably into the deep window recess, the better to enjoy their playful dance in the air.

Something startled me upright: the low, pitiful howling of dogs far below, in the valley hidden from my view. It seemed to grow louder in my ears, and the floating dust began forming new shapes in time with it as it danced through the moonlight. I felt myself struggling to wake in response to some instinctive warning. More than that: my very soul struggled, and my half-awakened senses tried to answer the call. I was being hypnotised! The dust danced faster and faster. Moonbeams seemed to tremble as they passed me into the darkness behind. The particles gathered more thickly until vague, ghostlike shapes appeared. Then I sprang fully awake, in complete possession of my senses, and fled screaming. Those phantom shapes, gradually taking substance from the moonlight, were the three spectral women to whom I was condemned. I ran to my own room and felt somewhat safer there: no moonlight entered, and the lamp burned brightly.

Two hours or so later, I heard movement in the Count’s room, followed by something like a sharp cry abruptly stifled. Then silence fell—deep, dreadful silence that chilled me. My heart pounding, I tried the door. But I remained locked in my prison, helpless to do anything. I sat down and simply wept.

While I sat there, a sound came from the courtyard: a woman’s agonised cry. I rushed to the window, flung it open and peered between the bars. A woman stood below with disordered hair, her hands clasped over her heart as if exhausted from running. She leaned against a corner of the gateway. Seeing my face at the window, she lunged forward and shouted threateningly:—
“Monster, give me back my child!”

She dropped to her knees and lifted her hands, repeating the words in a voice that tore at my heart. Then she pulled at her hair and beat her breast, giving herself over to violent, uncontrollable grief. At last she flung herself forward. I could no longer see her, but heard her bare hands pounding against the door.

Far above me, probably on the tower, I heard the Count call out in his harsh, metallic whisper. Wolves seemed to answer from every direction, far and wide. Within minutes a pack poured through the broad gateway into the courtyard, like water released from a dam.
The woman made no cry, and the wolves howled only briefly. Soon they filed away one by one, licking their lips.
I could feel no pity for her. Now I knew what had happened to her child; she was better off dead.
What am I to do? What can I do? How can I escape this dreadful creature of darkness, night and terror?

25 June, morning.—Until a man has suffered through the night, he cannot know how precious and beautiful morning can become to his eyes and heart. When today’s sun rose high enough to touch the top of the great gateway opposite my window, that bright spot seemed like a place where the dove from the ark had landed. My fear slipped away like a garment of mist dissolving in the warmth. I must act somehow while daylight lends me courage. Last night one of my letters with a future date was posted—the first in that fatal sequence intended to erase every trace of my existence from the earth.
I must not dwell on that. Action!

It has always been after dark that I have been attacked, threatened, endangered or frightened in any way. I have yet to see the Count in daylight. Does he sleep while others are awake so that he can wake while they sleep? If only I could enter his room! But there is no possible route. The door is always locked; I cannot get through.

Yes, there is another route, if I dare attempt it. Where his body has passed, why should another body not follow? I have watched him crawl out of his window. Why should I not do the same and enter that way? The chances are desperate, but my need is more desperate still. I will risk it. At worst it can only mean death, and a man’s death differs from a calf’s. The dreaded life hereafter may still be open to me. God help me in what I am about to do! Farewell, Mina, if I fail. Farewell, my loyal friend and second father. Farewell, everyone—and last of all, Mina!

Later the same day.—I have attempted it and, with God’s help, returned safely to this room. I must record every detail in its proper order. While my courage held, I went straight to the south window and climbed onto the narrow stone ledge running along that side of the building. The stones are large and roughly shaped, and time has washed the mortar from between them. I removed my boots and ventured along that desperate route. I looked down once, to prepare myself against being overwhelmed by an unexpected glimpse of the terrible drop. After that I kept my eyes away. I knew roughly where the Count’s window lay and how far away it was, and worked towards it as the available handholds allowed. I did not grow dizzy—perhaps I was too excited—and in what seemed an absurdly short time I stood on its sill, trying to lift the sash. Yet I trembled with agitation when I bent down and slid feet first through the opening. I looked around for the Count and made a discovery that both surprised and delighted me: the room was empty! It contained only a few odd pieces of furniture that appeared never to have been used. Their style resembled the furniture in the south rooms, and dust covered everything. I searched for the key. It was not in the lock and I could find it nowhere. All I discovered was a huge heap of gold in a corner: Roman, British, Austrian, Hungarian, Greek and Turkish coins of every sort. A film of dust covered them, as if they had lain buried for a long time. Not one I noticed was under three hundred years old. There were chains and ornaments too, some set with jewels, but all ancient and tarnished.

A heavy door stood in one corner. I tried it: since I had found neither this room’s key nor the outer-door key that was my main objective, I had to search farther or waste all my efforts. It opened onto a stone passage leading to a steep spiral staircase. I descended cautiously, watching my footing in the darkness. Only narrow openings in the thick masonry admitted light. At the bottom lay a dark, tunnellike passage carrying a sickening smell of death—the smell of old earth freshly disturbed. As I followed it, the odour grew stronger and more oppressive. Finally I pulled open a heavy door standing slightly ajar and entered an old ruined chapel, evidently once used for burials. Its roof was broken, and steps in two places led down to vaults. The ground had recently been dug up, and the soil put into great wooden boxes, plainly those the Slovaks had brought. No one was there. I searched for another way out and found none. Then I examined every inch of the ground, determined not to miss a chance. I even descended into the vaults where the faint light barely reached, though the thought terrified my very soul. The first two contained only broken old coffins and heaps of dust. In the third, however, I discovered something.

The Count lay inside one of the great boxes—there were fifty altogether—on a mound of freshly dug earth! I could not tell whether he slept or was dead. His eyes were open and stonelike, yet lacked the glassy look of death; beneath their pallor his cheeks still had the warmth of life, and his lips remained as red as ever. Yet nothing moved. There was no pulse, no breathing, no heartbeat. Leaning over him, I searched for any sign of life and found none. He could not have been there long: within a few hours the smell of disturbed earth would have faded. Beside the box lay its lid, pierced with holes. I thought he might carry the keys, but as I approached to search him, I saw those dead eyes. Dead though they were, and unaware of me or my presence, they held such hatred that I fled. I left his room by the window and crawled back up the castle wall. Once in my own room I flung myself onto the bed, panting, and tried to think....

29 June.—Today is the date on my final letter. The Count has arranged evidence of its authenticity: once again I watched him leave through the same window wearing my clothes. As he crept down the wall like a lizard, I longed for a gun or some other deadly weapon with which to destroy him. Yet I fear no weapon made by human hands alone could harm him. I dared not wait for his return, afraid of seeing those weird sisters. Instead I went back to the library and read until I fell asleep.
The Count woke me. His expression was as grim as any man’s could be as he spoke:—

“Tomorrow we must part, my friend. You will return to your beautiful England; I must undertake work whose outcome may mean we never meet again. Your letter home has been sent. Tomorrow I shall be absent, but everything will be prepared for your departure. The Szgany come in the morning to carry out some tasks here, and some Slovaks will arrive as well. Once they have left, my carriage will collect you and take you to the Borgo Pass, to meet the stagecoach travelling from Bukovina to Bistritz. Still, I hope we shall see more of each other at Castle Dracula.” I distrusted him and decided to test his sincerity. Sincerity! To use the word of such a monster seems almost a desecration. I asked him directly:—
“Why can I not leave tonight?”
“Because, my dear sir, my driver and horses are away carrying out an errand.”
“But I would gladly walk. I want to leave at once.” His smile was so gentle, so smooth and so devilish that I knew some trick lay behind that manner. He said:—
“What about your luggage?”
“It does not matter to me. I can arrange to have it sent later.”
The Count rose and spoke with such gracious politeness that I rubbed my eyes; it seemed entirely sincere:—

“You English have a saying dear to me, for it expresses the principle of our boyars: ‘Welcome the coming; speed the parting guest.’ Come with me, my dear young friend. You shall not remain in my house against your wishes for a single hour, though I am sorry you are leaving and that your desire to go is so sudden. Come!” Carrying the lamp with solemn dignity, he led me downstairs and along the hall. Abruptly he stopped.
“Listen!”

Many wolves began howling close by. Their cries seemed almost to spring from the lifting of his hand, just as a great orchestra’s music leaps into life beneath its conductor’s baton. After a short pause he continued to the door with the same stately manner, slid back the massive bolts, removed the heavy chains and started opening it.
To my utter astonishment, the door was not locked. I searched around suspiciously with my eyes, but could see no key anywhere.

As the door opened, the wolves outside howled louder and more fiercely. Through the widening gap came red jaws with snapping teeth and blunt-clawed feet as they leapt. I understood then that resisting the Count was useless for the moment. With allies like these under his command, he left me helpless. Still the door slowly opened farther, and only his body filled the gap. Suddenly I realised this might be how and when I was to die: delivered to the wolves at my own request. The idea had a devilish cruelty worthy of him. In a final attempt to save myself, I cried:—

“Close the door! I will wait until morning!” I hid my face in my hands to conceal tears of bitter disappointment. A single sweep of his powerful arm slammed the door shut. The great bolts clanged back into place, their echoes ringing through the hall.

We went back to the library without speaking. After a minute or two I left for my room. My last sight of Count Dracula was of him blowing me a kiss, a red gleam of triumph in his eyes and a smile that Judas himself might have worn proudly in hell.
I had reached my room and was about to lie down when I thought I heard whispers outside the door. I approached quietly and listened. Unless my ears were mistaken, the Count was speaking:—

“Back! Back to your own place! Your time has not arrived. Wait! Be patient! Tonight belongs to me. Tomorrow night belongs to you!” A low ripple of sweet laughter followed. Furious, I flung open the door. The three dreadful women stood outside, licking their lips. When they saw me, they burst into horrible laughter together and ran away.
I returned to my room and fell to my knees. Can the end be so close? Tomorrow! Tomorrow! Lord, help me, and help those who love me!

30 June, morning.—These may be the final words I ever set down in this diary. I slept until shortly before dawn. On waking, I dropped to my knees, determined that if Death came, he would find me prepared.

At last I felt that slight change in the air and knew morning had arrived. Then came the welcome crow of a cock, and I felt safe. My heart lifted. I opened my door and ran down to the hall. I had seen the outer door unlocked: now I could escape. My hands shook with eagerness as I unhooked the chains and slid back the enormous bolts.

But the door refused to move. Despair gripped me. I pulled and pulled, shaking it until, huge as it was, it rattled in its frame. I could see the lock’s bolt in place. It had been locked after I left the Count.

A frantic determination seized me: I would get that key, whatever the risk. I resolved to climb the wall again and reach the Count’s room. He might kill me, but death now seemed the happier of the evils before me. Without hesitation I rushed to the east window and scrambled down the wall into his room as before. It was empty, as I had expected. No key was visible anywhere, though the heap of gold remained. I passed through the corner door, descended the spiral stairs and followed the dark passage to the old chapel. By now I knew exactly where to find the monster I was seeking.

The great box remained beside the wall in the same place. Its lid had been laid on top, not yet fixed, with nails positioned ready to be hammered in. I knew I must search the body for the key, so I lifted the lid and propped it against the wall. What I saw filled my soul with horror. The Count lay there looking partly restored to youth. His white hair and moustache had turned dark iron-grey; his cheeks were fuller, and beneath the white skin seemed to glow a ruby red. His mouth was redder than ever. Fresh clots of blood clung to his lips, trickling from the corners over his chin and neck. Even the deep, burning eyes appeared buried in swollen flesh: their lids and the bags beneath them were bloated. The whole dreadful creature seemed gorged with blood. He lay like a filthy leech, exhausted by its own gluttony. I shuddered as I bent to touch him; every sense revolted. But I had to search or be lost. By the coming night, my own body might become just such a feast for those three horrors. I felt all over him and found no trace of a key. Then I stopped and stared. A mocking smile on that bloated face nearly drove me mad. This was the creature I was helping move to London! Among its millions he might satisfy his thirst for blood for centuries, creating an ever-growing circle of half-demons to feed upon the helpless. The thought maddened me. I felt a terrible urge to rid the world of him. There was no deadly weapon nearby, but I seized a shovel the workmen had used to fill the boxes. Raising it high, I struck at that hateful face with its edge. As I struck, however, his head turned. His eyes looked straight into mine, blazing with the horror of a basilisk. The sight seemed to paralyse me. The shovel twisted in my hand and glanced off his face, doing no more than cut a deep gash above his forehead. It fell from my grasp across the box. When I pulled it away, the projecting edge of its blade caught the lid and brought it down again, hiding the hideous creature. My last glimpse was of the swollen, bloodstained face fixed in a malicious grin worthy of the deepest hell.

I tried again and again to decide my next move, but my brain felt on fire. I waited, sinking into despair. Then I heard distant voices singing a cheerful gipsy song and coming closer. Through the singing came the rumble of heavy wheels and the crack of whips. These were the Szgany and Slovaks the Count had mentioned. After one last look around and at the box holding that vile body, I ran back to the Count’s room, determined to dash out the moment the door opened. Straining to listen, I heard a key grate in the great lock downstairs, then the heavy door swing back. There must be another entrance, or someone possessed a key to one of the locked doors. Many footsteps followed, marching away down a passage that echoed with a metallic clang. I turned to hurry towards the vault again, hoping to find this new way in. At that moment a violent gust seemed to blow through. The door to the winding stairs slammed shut so hard that dust flew from its lintel. I rushed to push it open, but it was stuck beyond hope. Once again I was a prisoner, with the net of doom tightening around me.

As I write, I hear many feet tramping through the passage below and heavy objects crashing down—surely the boxes carrying their loads of earth. Now there is hammering: they are nailing the box shut. Now the heavy footsteps pass along the hall again, followed by many others whose owners bear no burden.
The door closes and the chains rattle. A key grates in the lock; I hear it being withdrawn. Then another door opens and closes, followed by the creak of a lock and bolt.
Listen! Heavy wheels roll across the courtyard and down the rocky path. Whips crack, and the Szgany sing together as they recede into the distance.
I am alone in the castle with those dreadful women. Ugh! Mina is a woman, and they share nothing with her. They are devils from the Pit!

I will not stay here alone with them. I will try to climb farther along the castle wall than I have yet dared. I shall carry some gold in case I need it later. Perhaps I can find a way out of this terrible place.
Then away towards home! To the nearest train, the fastest train! Away from this accursed place and country, where the devil and his children still walk the earth on mortal feet!
At least God has more mercy than these monsters, and the precipice is high and steep. At its foot a man may sleep—as a man. Farewell, everyone! Mina!

chapters.title: Chapter V
paragraphs: Letter from Miss Mina Murray to Miss Lucy Westenra.
“9 May.
“My dearest Lucy,—

“Please forgive me for taking so long to write. Work has quite overwhelmed me. Being an assistant schoolteacher can be trying at times. How I long to be with you beside the sea, talking freely and building our castles in the air! Lately I have worked especially hard because I want to keep pace with Jonathan’s studies, and I have been practising shorthand diligently. Once we are married, I shall be able to help him. If my shorthand becomes good enough, I can take down what he wants to say and type it out for him. I am working hard at the typewriter too. Sometimes we exchange shorthand letters, and he is using shorthand for the journal of his travels abroad. I shall keep a diary in the same way when I come to stay with you. I don’t mean one of those diaries that allow two pages for a week and squeeze Sunday into a corner, but a journal where I can write whenever I choose. I doubt other people would find much to interest them, but it is not meant for them. Perhaps I shall show Jonathan something worth sharing one day; really, though, it will be a book for practice. I want to imitate women journalists: conduct interviews, describe things, and try to recall conversations. Apparently, with a little practice, one can remember everything that happens or is said within one’s hearing in a day. We shall see. When we meet, I shall explain all my little plans. A few hurried lines from Jonathan have just arrived from Transylvania. He is well and expects to come home in about a week. I cannot wait to hear everything he has to tell me. How lovely it must be to visit unfamiliar countries! I wonder whether we—Jonathan and I, I mean—will ever travel to them together. The ten o’clock bell is ringing. Goodbye.
“With love from
“MINA.
“Write and tell me all your news. You have told me nothing for ages. I hear rumours, especially about a tall, handsome man with curly hair???
Letter from Lucy Westenra to Mina Murray.
“17, Chatham Street,
“Wednesday.
“My dearest Mina,—

“Really, it is very unfair of you to accuse me of neglecting my letters. I have written twice since we parted, and your last letter was only your second! Besides, I have no news—certainly nothing that would interest you. London is delightful at present. We often visit picture galleries, and walk or ride in the park. As for the tall man with curly hair, I suppose you mean the one who accompanied me to the last Pop concert. Clearly someone has been carrying tales. That was Mr. Holmwood. He visits often, and he and mamma get along beautifully; they have so many shared interests to discuss. A while ago we met a man who would suit you perfectly if you were not already engaged to Jonathan. He is a most desirable match: handsome, wealthy and well born. He is also a doctor, and very clever. Imagine—he is only twenty-nine, yet has the whole charge of an enormous lunatic asylum! Mr. Holmwood introduced us. He came to call afterwards and now visits regularly. I think he is among the most determined men I have ever met, and also among the calmest. Nothing seems capable of disturbing him. I can imagine the remarkable influence he must have over his patients. He has a curious way of looking directly into your face, as if he means to read your thoughts. He tries it constantly with me, but I flatter myself that he has found a difficult puzzle. My mirror tells me so. Do you ever try to read your own expression? I do, and I assure you it makes a worthwhile study. If you have never tried, you cannot imagine how much trouble it gives you. He says I offer him a curious psychological case, and I humbly agree. As you know, I care too little about clothes to describe the latest fashions. Clothes are a bore. There I go using slang again, but never mind: Arthur says it daily. There, I have let everything out! Mina, we have shared every secret since childhood. We have slept and eaten together, laughed and cried together. Now that I have started, I want to say more. Oh, Mina, haven’t you guessed? I love him. I am blushing as I write. Although I think he loves me, he has never actually said so. But oh, Mina, I love him; I love him; I love him! There—that makes me feel better. I wish I were with you, dear, sitting by the fire as we undressed, the way we used to. I would try to explain what I feel. I hardly know how I can write this even to you. I dare not stop, or I might tear up the letter. And I don’t want to stop, because I want so much to tell you everything. Answer at once and tell me exactly what you think. Mina, I must finish. Goodnight. Remember me in your prayers, and, Mina, pray that I may be happy.
“LUCY.
“P.S.—You hardly need telling that this is a secret. Goodnight again.
Letter from Lucy Westenra to Mina Murray.
“24 May.
“My dearest Mina,—
“Thank you, thank you, and thank you again for your lovely letter. What a comfort it was to tell you everything and feel your sympathy.

“My dear, it never rains but it pours! Those old sayings are so true. I turn twenty in September and had never received a proposal—not a real one—until today. Today I have had three. Can you imagine? THREE proposals in a single day! Isn’t it dreadful! I feel sorry, truly and honestly sorry, for two of those poor men. Oh, Mina, I am so happy I hardly know what to do with myself. And three proposals! For goodness’ sake, though, don’t tell any of the girls. They would develop the wildest expectations and feel insulted and ill-used unless they received at least six on their first day at home. Some girls are terribly vain! You and I, dear Mina, engaged and soon to settle into sensible old married women, can look down on vanity. Well, I must describe all three, but you must keep it secret from everyone, dear—except Jonathan, of course. You will tell him, because in your place I would certainly tell Arthur. A woman ought to tell her husband everything, don’t you agree? And I must be fair. Men expect women, certainly their wives, to be as fair as they are themselves. I fear we women are not always as fair as we should be. Well, dear, number One arrived just before lunch. I have already described him: Dr. John Seward, the asylum doctor, with his firm jaw and fine forehead. He appeared perfectly calm, but underneath he was nervous. He had clearly rehearsed all sorts of small details and remembered them. Yet he almost sat on his silk hat, which is hardly what a composed man does. Then, trying to seem relaxed, he kept fiddling with a lancet until I nearly screamed. He spoke very plainly, Mina. He told me how much I meant to him despite our short acquaintance, and what his life could become with me to help and encourage him. He began describing how miserable he would be if I could not care for him, but when I cried, he called himself a brute and said he would not increase my distress. Breaking off, he asked whether I might learn to love him. I shook my head, and his hands trembled. After some hesitation he asked if I already cared for somebody else. He put it delicately: he did not wish to force a confidence from me, only to know whether my heart was free, because then a man could still hope. Mina, I felt I owed him the truth that there was someone. That was all I told him. He stood up, looking so strong and solemn, and took both my hands. He wished me happiness and said that if I ever needed a friend, I must count him among my best. Oh, dear Mina, I cannot stop crying; forgive all the blots on this letter. Proposals are very pleasant, and all that, but it is no pleasure to watch a poor man who truly loves you leave utterly heartbroken. Whatever he may say at that moment, you know you are passing out of his life. My dear, I must stop for now. I feel so miserable, though I am so happy.
“Evening.

“Arthur has just left, and I feel more cheerful than when I stopped writing, so I can continue the day’s story. Number Two came after lunch, my dear. Such a lovely man, an American from Texas. He looks so young and fresh that it is hard to believe all the places he has visited and the adventures he has had. I understand poor Desdemona, listening to such a stream of dangers, even from a black man. Perhaps we women are such cowards that we marry a man because we think he will rescue us from our fears. Now I know what I would do if I were a man who wanted a girl to love him. No, I don’t: Mr. Morris told us all his stories, and Arthur never told any, and yet— My dear, I am getting ahead of myself. Mr. Quincey P. Morris found me alone. Men always seem to find a girl alone. No, they don’t: Arthur tried twice to create an opportunity, with all the help I could give him. I am not ashamed to admit that now. First I should explain that Mr. Morris does not always use slang. He never does with strangers, or in their presence; he is very well educated and has exquisite manners. But he discovered that his American slang amused me. Whenever I was there, with nobody who might be shocked, he would say the funniest things. I suspect he invents it all, dear, because it fits whatever else he wants to say so exactly. But slang is like that. I wonder whether I shall ever use it myself. I do not know if Arthur likes it, as I have not yet heard him use any. Well, Mr. Morris sat beside me looking as happy and cheerful as he could, though I saw quite clearly that he was very nervous. He took my hand and said, ever so sweetly:—

“‘Miss Lucy, I know I ain’t fit even to see to the fixin’s on your little shoes. But I reckon if you wait for a man who is, you’ll end up joining those seven young women with the lamps when your time is up. Won’t you hitch up beside me, and let us travel that long road together in double harness?’

“He looked so cheerful and good-natured that refusing him seemed much easier than refusing poor Dr. Seward. So I said, as lightly as possible, that I knew nothing about hitching and had not been broken to harness yet. Then he admitted that he had spoken playfully. He hoped I would forgive him if that had been wrong on an occasion so serious and important to him. He looked truly earnest as he said it, and I could not help becoming a little serious too. I know, Mina, you will call me a dreadful flirt, but I still felt a little thrill that he was the second that day. Then, before I could answer, he poured out a whole flood of declarations, laying his heart and soul at my feet. He was so sincere that I shall never again assume that a man who is sometimes merry must always be playful and never serious. Something in my face must have stopped him. He broke off suddenly and spoke with a manly warmth that could have made me love him, had I been free:—

“‘Lucy, I know you’re an honest-hearted girl. I wouldn’t be standing here speaking this way if I didn’t believe you were pure grit, right down to the bottom of your soul. Tell me, one good fellow to another: is there somebody else you care for? If there is, I won’t trouble you one little bit again. But if you’ll allow it, I’ll be a faithful friend.’

“My dear Mina, why are men so noble when we women deserve them so little? I had almost been teasing this generous, true gentleman. I burst into tears—dear, you will think this a very sloppy letter in more senses than one—and felt thoroughly ashamed. Why can’t a girl marry three men, or however many want her, and spare everyone this misery? But that is heresy; I must not say it. I am glad that even through my tears I could look into Mr. Morris’s brave eyes and answer directly:—

“‘Yes, I love someone, though he has not yet even told me he loves me.’ I was right to speak to him so honestly. His face brightened, and he held out both hands to take mine—or perhaps I placed mine in his. He said warmly:—

“‘That’s my brave girl. Arriving too late for a chance of winning you is worth more than arriving in time for any other girl alive. Don’t cry, dear. If those tears are for me, I’m tough to crack, and I can take it on my feet. If that other fellow doesn’t recognise his good fortune, he’d better wake up soon, or he’ll have me to answer to. Little girl, your honesty and courage have made me your friend. That’s rarer than a lover, and more unselfish, anyway. I’ve a pretty lonely road ahead, my dear, from here to Kingdom Come. Could you give me one kiss? It would help hold back the darkness now and then. You can if you want: that other good fellow—he must be good, and a fine man too, or you couldn’t love him—hasn’t spoken yet.’ That won me completely, Mina. Wasn’t it brave and sweet of him, and generous towards his rival, even when he was so unhappy? I leaned forward and kissed him. He stood up, still holding both my hands, and looked down into my face—I fear I was blushing terribly—and said:—

“‘Little girl, I’m holding your hand, and you’ve kissed me. If that doesn’t make us friends, nothing will. Thank you for being so kindly honest with me. Goodbye.’ He squeezed my hand, picked up his hat and walked straight out without looking back, without a tear, a tremor or a pause. And here I am, crying like a baby. Oh, why should a man like that suffer when so many girls would worship the ground he walked on? I know I would, if I were free—only I do not want to be free. It has quite upset me, dear. After telling you this, I cannot immediately write about happiness, and I want the story of number Three to be entirely happy.
“Always with love from
“LUCY.

“P.S.—Oh, number Three! I hardly need to tell you about number Three, do I? Besides, everything was such a blur. He seemed scarcely to have entered the room before both his arms were around me and he was kissing me. I am so very, very happy, and I cannot imagine what I have done to earn it. All I can do is try, from now on, to show God my gratitude for His kindness in sending me such a lover, such a husband and such a friend.
“Goodbye.”
Dr. Seward’s Diary.
(Recorded on a phonograph)

25 May.—Appetite at low tide today. Cannot eat or rest, so I turn to the diary. Yesterday’s rejection has left me feeling empty; nothing in the world seems important enough to be worth doing.... Knowing work was the only cure, I went down among the patients. I chose one whose case has given me a particularly interesting study. He is so peculiar that I am determined to understand him as thoroughly as possible. Today I felt I came closer than ever to the centre of his mystery.

I questioned him more closely than before, hoping to establish all the facts of his hallucination. Looking back, I can see a certain cruelty in my method. I seemed to want to hold him at the very point of his madness—something I normally avoid with patients as I would the entrance to hell.

(Note: under what circumstances would I not avoid the pit of hell?) Omnia Romæ venalia sunt. Everything in Rome is for sale. Hell has its price! Verb. sap.—a word to the wise. If there is something behind this instinct, it will be worth tracing accurately later. I had better begin that record now. Therefore—

R. M. Renfield, aged 59.—Sanguine temperament; exceptional physical strength; morbid excitability; periods of depression ending in a fixed idea I cannot identify. I suppose his sanguine nature and the influence disturbing him find their eventual outcome within his mind. A potentially dangerous man; probably dangerous if unselfish. Selfish men’s caution protects their enemies as effectively as themselves. My thought is this: when the self is the fixed centre, the inward and outward forces balance. When duty, a cause or something similar becomes the fixed centre, the outward force dominates. Only chance, or a sequence of chance events, can then restore the balance.
Letter from Quincey P. Morris to the Hon. Arthur Holmwood.
“25 May.
“My dear Art,—

“We’ve swapped yarns around prairie campfires, dressed each other’s wounds after attempting a landing in the Marquesas, and drunk to one another on the shores of Titicaca. There are still stories to tell, other wounds to mend, and another toast to drink. Will you join us around my campfire tomorrow night for that? I ask without hesitation, knowing a certain lady is promised to a certain dinner party and you are therefore free. There will be just one other guest: our old friend from the Korea, Jack Seward. He is coming too. We want to mix our tears over the wine and drink wholeheartedly to the happiest man in this wide world, the man who has won the noblest heart God ever made, and the one most worth winning. You’ll find a warm welcome, an affectionate greeting and a toast as true as your own right hand. We will both promise to leave you at home if you drink too deeply to a certain pair of eyes. Come!
“Yours, now and always,
“QUINCEY P. MORRIS.”
Telegram from Arthur Holmwood to Quincey P. Morris.
“26 May.
“You can always count on me. I bring messages that will set both your ears tingling.
“ART.”
